title: CVE-2026-87862: HSTS cache import drops longer-lived child
excerpt:
# HSTS cache import silently drops a longer-lived child beneath an includeSubDomains parent

## Summary

Loading an HSTS cache (file or `CURLOPT_HSTSREADFUNCTION` callback) can silently discard a child entry. When a live `includeSubDomains` parent is imported before a longer-lived `includeSubDomains` child, only the parent is retained. After the parent expires, the child's independently valid HSTS policy is gone and curl sends a plaintext HTTP request instead of upgrading to HTTPS. This violates the independent-policy model required by RFC 6797 §5.3.

## Affected versions

The file-load path regressed in commit `a94973805df96269bf3f3bf0a20ccb9887313316` (CVE-2024-9681 fix), first released in curl 8.11.0. The callback-load path inherited the same logic in commit `e65ba1bd349a7affb09275a442b6a0837df079d9`, released in curl 8.20.0. Verified at `c2676bf9e639e31e44b12a2cc82cf2046231b056`.

## Root cause

`hsts_add_host_expire()` in `lib/hsts.c` calls `hsts_check(h, host, hostlen, subdomain)` with `subdomain=TRUE` at line 464. `hsts_check()` performs hierarchical matching: if the parent `.example.test` is already loaded with `includeSubDomains`, it returns the parent as a match for `child.example.test`. The caller creates an entry only when no match exists, and its update branch runs only when the returned hostname exactly matches the imported hostname. An ancestor match therefore causes neither an update nor a creation — the child is silently dropped.

Network-learned `Strict-Transport-Security` processing does not have this problem because `Curl_hsts_parse()` uses exact-only lookup (`hsts_check(..., FALSE)`) at line 296.

## Reproduction steps
Build curl from current master (or any version since 8.11.0) with HSTS support enabled and ENABLE_DEBUG=ON (for CURL_TIME clock control).
Create an HSTS cache file with two includeSubDomains entries where the parent is listed first and the child has a later expiry, e.g.:
.example.test "20241010 00:00:00"
.child.example.test "20251010 00:00:00"
Set the clock to a time when both entries are still valid (e.g. CURL_TIME=1728465947, October 2024).
Run any curl request with --hsts <cache-file> to force curl to load and rewrite the cache.
Inspect the rewritten cache file — it now contains only one entry (the parent). The child entry has been silently dropped.

key_reasons: The code at lib/hsts.c:464 calls hsts_check with subdomain=TRUE during cache import, enabling hierarchical matching for deduplication.
hsts_check (lines 190-198) returns a parent includeSubDomains entry as a match for a child hostname.
The subsequent exact-match check (lines 470-471) fails because hostnames differ, so the child is neither created nor updated — it is silently dropped.
Network-learned policy processing (Curl_hsts_parse at line 296) correctly uses exact-only lookup (FALSE) for the same purpose.

After the parent expires, the child's independently valid HSTS policy is gone, causing plaintext HTTP requests where HTTPS upgrade should occur — a security impact per RFC 6797's independent-policy model.
reply: The report is correct: hsts_add_host_expire() at lib/hsts.c:464 uses hierarchical matching (subdomain=TRUE) for import deduplication, which silently drops a longer-lived child when a parent with includeSubDomains is already present. The fix — changing that call to subdomain=FALSE to match Curl_hsts_parse() at line 296 — is sound. This affects released versions from 8.11.0 onward. Thank you for the clear analysis and reproduction steps.
